subtopic_detail: A sixteen year old who cannot fall asleep until the early hours and cannot be woken for school but sleeps normally through the holidays
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 16 year old boy brought by his mother, who has been told by the school that he is depressed and needs antidepressants. He has missed 14 days of school this term because he cannot be woken in the morning.

He tells you he lies awake until about 3 am no matter when he goes to bed, then sleeps soundly until midday if left alone. He feels dreadful and irritable when dragged up at 7 am but says he feels fine by mid afternoon. Over the recent three week holiday he slept from 3 am to 11 am and reported that his mood and energy were good throughout. He enjoys football and sees friends most weekends. He denies any loss of interest, hopelessness or thoughts of self harm, and his weight is stable. He drinks no caffeine after lunch and uses his phone in bed until he falls asleep.

data_table.Examination: Alert and engaged during an afternoon appointment, normal affect with reactive range, no psychomotor retardation, no signs of self harm
data_table.Investigations: Sleep diary over two weeks showing consistent sleep onset between 2.30 and 3.30 am and spontaneous waking between 11 am and midday on free days, full blood count within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, ferritin 62 micrograms/L (30 to 300)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Prescribe an antidepressant and arrange psychology review in four weeks
options.rationale: A depressive episode requires persistent low mood or loss of interest, and his mood and energy were good throughout a holiday during which he slept the same total hours at his own preferred times. Treating the mislabelled diagnosis exposes him to medication while leaving the timing problem untouched. (Source: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents

options.text: Advise a fixed earlier bedtime with the phone removed from the bedroom
options.rationale: Removing screens and setting a consistent schedule are worthwhile components but on their own they simply lengthen the time he lies awake, because the underlying circadian phase has not been shifted. Sleep hygiene alone is appropriate where the difficulty is behavioural rather than a delayed body clock. (Source: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents

options.text: Refer for overnight polysomnography before starting any treatment
options.rationale: A sleep study measures sleep architecture and breathing and is indicated when obstructive sleep apnoea, a parasomnia or narcolepsy is suspected, none of which fits a boy who sleeps soundly and unbroken for eight or nine hours once asleep. The diagnosis here is made from the sleep diary rather than from laboratory monitoring. (Source: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents

options.text: Give low dose melatonin in the early evening with morning bright light
options.rationale: Preserved sleep quality and duration with a consistently shifted timing that normalises on free days identifies a delayed circadian phase, and treatment combines a small melatonin dose several hours before his current sleep onset to advance the clock with timed bright light on waking to consolidate the shift. Sleep scheduling and screen advice are added alongside rather than instead of this. (Source: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents

options.text: Start a sedative hypnotic at night and review his progress in two weeks
options.rationale: Hypnotics have no role in a circadian timing disorder and do not advance the phase, so waking remains as difficult while dependence and next day sedation become new problems. They are not recommended for adolescent insomnia in Australian practice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder is the commonest circadian rhythm disorder of adolescence and reflects a genuine biological shift in the timing of the sleep-wake cycle at puberty, amplified by evening light exposure and social schedules. It is routinely mistaken for depression, school refusal or laziness, and the distinguishing feature is that sleep itself is normal in quality and duration whenever the young person is allowed to sleep at their preferred times, which is why performance during school holidays is such a useful piece of history. The consequences of missing the diagnosis are substantial, since chronic sleep restriction on school days produces irritability, poor concentration and low mood that can then be treated as a primary mood disorder. Treatment advances the circadian phase using small doses of melatonin timed several hours before habitual sleep onset for its chronobiotic rather than hypnotic effect, combined with bright light on waking, gradual advancement of the schedule and reduced evening light, and relapse is common when holidays allow the phase to drift back.
key_points: Normal sleep quality and duration at preferred times is the diagnostic clue
Performance during school holidays separates this from a depressive episode
Melatonin is used for its phase advancing effect, not as a hypnotic
Timed morning bright light consolidates the shift
Relapse after holidays is common and warrants a maintenance plan
explanation.pearls: Melatonin advances the clock only when given several hours before habitual sleep onset, so a dose taken at the current 3 am bedtime is useless and a dose of around 0.5 to 1 mg taken in the early evening is what shifts the phase; larger doses act as sedatives without improving the phase advance.

sources.label: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
Australasian Sleep Association: Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders

subtopic_detail: Writhing tongue and lip movements developing after years of haloperidol in a man already taking benztropine for stiffness
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 54 year old man with schizophrenia who has taken haloperidol 10 mg daily for nine years. Benztropine 2 mg daily was added six years ago for muscle stiffness and has been continued since.

Over the past four months his wife has noticed continuous movements of his tongue and lips. He is largely unaware of them. His psychotic symptoms have been well controlled for several years and he takes his medication reliably. On examination there are continuous writhing movements of the tongue with lip smacking and intermittent grimacing, plus occasional choreiform movements of the fingers. The movements lessen briefly when you ask him to open his mouth and hold his tongue still, and increase when he is distracted by mental arithmetic. There is no cogwheel rigidity, no tremor and no subjective inner restlessness.

data_table.Examination: Continuous choreoathetoid movements of the tongue with lip smacking and intermittent grimacing, occasional choreiform finger movements, movements briefly suppressible on request and worse with distraction, no cogwheel rigidity, no resting tremor, no akathisia on questioning or observation
data_table.Investigations: Urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Increase the benztropine dose to control the abnormal movements
options.rationale: Anticholinergic medication reliably worsens these movements rather than relieving them, so increasing it aggravates the very problem being treated. Benztropine is effective for acute dystonia and drug induced parkinsonism, which are different movement disorders with a different mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add propranolol and continue his current medications unchanged
options.rationale: A beta blocker is a treatment for akathisia, and he specifically denies inner restlessness and shows none on observation. Choosing a treatment for the wrong drug induced movement disorder leaves the causative regimen untouched. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Withdraw the benztropine and switch him to a different antipsychotic
options.rationale: Anticholinergics unmask and worsen tardive movements so benztropine is withdrawn slowly, and the causative high potency first generation antipsychotic is switched to an agent with lower tardive liability, with clozapine carrying the strongest evidence where the movements are severe or the illness has been difficult to treat. Abrupt cessation of the antipsychotic is avoided because withdrawal can transiently worsen the movements and destabilise the psychosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Stop the haloperidol abruptly today and review him again next week
options.rationale: Sudden withdrawal risks relapse of a psychotic illness that has been stable for years and can transiently worsen the movements through withdrawal emergent dyskinesia. A planned cross taper to a lower liability agent achieves the same aim safely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange genetic testing and brain imaging for an inherited chorea
options.rationale: Huntington disease would be considered where there is a family history, cognitive decline or a progressive chorea without a plausible drug cause, and here nine years of a high potency antipsychotic provides that cause. Investigation is reserved for atypical features rather than a classic orofacial drug induced picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Tardive dyskinesia is a delayed onset movement disorder characterised by choreoathetoid movements that favour the orofacial region, and it emerges after months to years of dopamine receptor blockade with a higher incidence for first generation agents, in older patients and in those with longer cumulative exposure. It must be separated from the other drug induced movement disorders because the treatments diverge sharply: acute dystonia and parkinsonism respond to anticholinergics, akathisia to dose reduction with propranolol or a benzodiazepine, while anticholinergics actively worsen tardive movements. The mainstays of management are recognition and dose review, withdrawal of anticholinergic medication, and a switch to an antipsychotic with lower tardive liability, with clozapine having the best evidence for improvement in established cases. Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitors such as valbenazine and deutetrabenazine are effective and are used internationally, although Australian access is limited, and tetrabenazine is an alternative that carries a risk of depression. Movements can be irreversible, which is why routine surveillance with a structured examination is recommended for anyone on long term antipsychotic treatment.
key_points: Orofacial choreoathetosis after prolonged dopamine blockade defines the syndrome
Anticholinergics worsen tardive movements and must be withdrawn
Propranolol treats akathisia, a different drug induced movement disorder
Switch to a lower liability agent; clozapine has the best evidence in established cases
Abrupt antipsychotic withdrawal risks relapse and withdrawal emergent dyskinesia
explanation.pearls: The bedside discriminator is the effect of distraction: tardive movements increase when the patient performs mental arithmetic and can be briefly suppressed voluntarily, whereas drug induced parkinsonian tremor lessens with distraction and increases with sustained posture.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia
BMJ Best Practice: Tardive dyskinesia

subtopic_detail: A fifteen year old playing online until dawn with falling grades and rage when the console is removed, whose parents want the internet cut off
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 15 year old boy with his parents, who are exhausted and want the home internet disconnected. Over the past year he has played online games for eight to ten hours most days, often until dawn, and his school reports have fallen from solid passes to failures.

He has stopped attending football and no longer sees the friends he used to. He becomes verbally abusive and once punched a door when his father removed the console. He denies low mood and says he would be fine if everyone left him alone, though he admits he has tried to cut back several times and could not. He has lost 3 kg and often skips breakfast to keep playing. He uses no alcohol or other drugs and there is no history of gambling or in-game purchasing.

data_table.Examination: Slim, tired looking, engaged and articulate when discussing gaming, reactive affect with no psychomotor change, no evidence of intoxication or withdrawal, no self harm marks
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 48 micrograms/L (30 to 300), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, HbA1c within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management approach?

options.text: Support the parents to disconnect the internet at home immediately
options.rationale: Abrupt unilateral removal of access commonly escalates conflict and aggression without building the self regulation the young person needs, and it forfeits his engagement in treatment. Negotiated graded limits achieve better adherence than a unilateral cut off. (Source: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people)
source_refs: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people

options.text: Refer for family based behavioural therapy with a structured sleep and school plan
options.rationale: Management of problematic gaming in an adolescent is psychosocial and family centred, combining negotiated graded reduction in screen time, restoration of sleep and school attendance, reintroduction of the activities and friendships he has dropped, and work with the parents on consistent limits. Screening for a co-occurring mood, anxiety or attention disorder happens alongside this because those conditions are frequently present and change the plan. (Source: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people)
source_refs: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in four weeks
options.rationale: There is no evidence base for pharmacotherapy of gaming behaviour itself, and he does not describe a depressive or anxiety syndrome that would independently warrant an antidepressant. Medication becomes relevant if a treatable comorbid disorder is identified on assessment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reassure the parents that this is a normal phase of adolescent development
options.rationale: Heavy gaming is common in adolescence and usually needs no intervention, but functional collapse across school, sleep, nutrition, friendships and family relationships is what distinguishes a disorder from a hobby. Normalising this level of impairment delays effective help. (Source: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people)
source_refs: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people

options.text: Refer him to a residential drug and alcohol withdrawal service for admission
options.rationale: He uses no substances, so a withdrawal service has nothing to treat and the model of care does not match the problem. Residential treatment is considered for severe refractory cases within specialist mental health services rather than as an initial step. (Source: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people)
source_refs: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people

explanation.summary: Gaming disorder is recognised in the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases and is defined by impaired control over gaming, escalating priority given to gaming over other activities, and continuation despite negative consequences, with significant functional impairment over at least twelve months in most cases. Prevalence estimates in Australian adolescents are low, in the order of a few per cent, which means most heavy gaming is not disorder and the assessment hinges on functional impact rather than hours played. Comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, depression, anxiety and social difficulties all over-represented, and gaming frequently serves as avoidance of an underlying problem such as bullying, social anxiety or undiagnosed learning difficulty. Treatment is psychological and family based, and the evidence favours graded negotiated reduction with restoration of sleep, education and offline social contact over abrupt prohibition, which tends to escalate conflict.
key_points: Functional impairment, not hours played, defines the disorder
Comorbid attention, mood and anxiety disorders are common and must be sought
Gaming often functions as avoidance of an underlying difficulty
Treatment is family based and psychosocial, not pharmacological
Graded negotiated reduction works better than abrupt removal of access
explanation.pearls: Sleep is the most productive first target, because restoring a consistent sleep window forces a reduction in overnight gaming while giving a visible early win, and the daytime irritability that parents attribute to withdrawal from gaming usually improves within two weeks of the sleep schedule holding.

sources.label: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
World Health Organization: International Classification of Diseases eleventh revision, gaming disorder

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of tearfulness and poor sleep after being made redundant in a man who still enjoys his weekends and has no diurnal variation
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 47 year old man three weeks after he was made redundant from a job he had held for eighteen years. He asks for antidepressants because he feels he is not coping.

He describes tearfulness when he thinks about telling his extended family, difficulty getting to sleep as he worries about the mortgage, and a preoccupation with how unfairly the process was handled. He still enjoys cycling at the weekend and went to a friend's birthday dinner last week and had a good time. He denies any diurnal variation in mood, no loss of appetite and no weight change, and his concentration is intact when he is doing something he chooses. He has no thoughts of self harm, no previous episodes of depression and no family history of mood disorder. He drinks two standard drinks most evenings, up from one.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when describing the redundancy but settles quickly and engages, affect reactive with preserved humour, no psychomotor retardation, speech and thought form normal, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, HbA1c within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start sertraline at 50 mg daily and review him again in two weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants have limited benefit in adjustment reactions where the symptoms are proportionate to a current stressor and anhedonia is absent, and starting one here medicalises a normal response while exposing him to side effects. An antidepressant becomes appropriate if he develops persistent anhedonia, diurnal variation or other features of a depressive episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine for his initial insomnia
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines risk dependence and are particularly unwise alongside increasing alcohol intake, and they do not address the financial worry keeping him awake. Their limited role is short term use for severe agitation or insomnia where non-drug measures have failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reassure him that no intervention is required and review in three months
options.rationale: His distress is genuine and is affecting sleep and family relationships, and his alcohol intake has risen, so leaving him without support for three months misses a chance to intervene early. Watchful waiting is reasonable for milder distress with intact sleep and no change in substance use. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer urgently to the acute mental health team for same day assessment
options.rationale: Urgent referral is driven by risk of harm to self or others, psychotic symptoms or severe functional collapse, and he has none of these with no suicidal ideation on direct questioning. Escalating care to this level would be disproportionate and would consume an acute service place. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Refer for structured problem solving therapy with review of his alcohol use
options.rationale: A distressing but proportionate reaction to an identifiable stressor with preserved capacity for enjoyment and no biological features of a depressive episode is best treated with structured psychological intervention aimed at the practical problems driving the distress, alongside brief intervention for his rising alcohol intake. Review is arranged so that an evolving depressive episode is picked up if the pattern changes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Distinguishing an adjustment disorder from a major depressive episode is one of the commonest and most consequential judgements in primary care mental health, because the treatments differ and antidepressants perform poorly when the diagnosis is wrong. The features that point towards a depressive episode are pervasive anhedonia, diurnal mood variation, early morning waking, appetite and weight change, psychomotor change, guilt and worthlessness beyond the circumstances, and suicidal ideation; the features that point towards adjustment are a clear temporal link to a stressor, distress that fluctuates with reminders of it, preserved capacity for pleasure, and symptoms that are understandable in proportion to the event. The correct management of adjustment reactions is psychological and practical, with structured problem solving and, where relevant, financial, legal or employment supports, since the stressor itself is often modifiable. Escalating alcohol use is a common and under-asked complication that predicts a worse trajectory and warrants brief intervention at the first visit, and follow up is scheduled because a proportion of adjustment presentations evolve into a depressive episode.
key_points: Preserved capacity for pleasure argues against a depressive episode
Diurnal variation, early morning waking and weight change point to depression
Antidepressants have limited benefit in proportionate reactions to a stressor
Structured problem solving targets the modifiable stressor
Rising alcohol use is common, predicts a worse course and warrants brief intervention
explanation.pearls: Asking specifically whether the person still enjoys the things they chose to do last weekend separates adjustment from a depressive episode more reliably than asking about mood, because anhedonia is the symptom that does not remit when the person is distracted from the stressor.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines
BMJ Best Practice: Adjustment disorder

subtopic_detail: A new father screening above threshold at the six week check with irritability and withdrawal while his partner is being treated for postnatal depression
stem:
You are the general practice registrar conducting the six week check for a baby girl. Her mother was diagnosed with postnatal depression two weeks ago and started sertraline. The baby's father, aged 33, has come to every appointment and today mentions in passing that he is not doing well either.

With his agreement you ask him more. For the past month he has felt persistently flat and unusually irritable, snapping at his partner and his older child. He has been working longer hours because he finds home overwhelming, has stopped playing indoor cricket and has been drinking four or five beers most nights, up from two on weekends. He describes waking at 4 am unable to get back to sleep, and says he no longer looks forward to anything. He scores 14 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale and answers no to the self harm item. He has no history of mental illness.

data_table.Examination: Flat affect with limited reactivity, slowed speech, appears tired, no psychomotor agitation, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation on direct questioning including the screening item
data_table.Investigations: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score 14 with a negative response to the self harm item, full blood count within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, liver function tests showing gamma glutamyl transferase 68 U/L (less than 60) with other enzymes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Explain that this scale is not validated in men and take no further action
options.rationale: The scale has been studied in fathers and performs acceptably, although a lower cut off is generally applied in men because they score lower for equivalent severity. Dismissing the result on validity grounds would leave a father with clear depressive symptoms untreated. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline

options.text: Arrange his own assessment and care plan, addressing his alcohol intake
options.rationale: A father with persistent low mood, anhedonia, early morning waking and rising alcohol use scoring above the male threshold has a depressive episode in his own right and needs a full assessment with a management plan in his name, including psychological therapy, consideration of an antidepressant and brief intervention for alcohol. Paternal depression independently affects infant development and the mother's recovery, so treating him is part of caring for the family rather than an aside. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline

options.text: Advise that his symptoms will settle once his partner's treatment works
options.rationale: Paternal depression is not simply a reaction to maternal illness and does not reliably remit when the mother improves, so deferring his care to her treatment response leaves him untreated for months. His anhedonia and early morning waking indicate an independent episode. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline

options.text: Refer the couple for relationship counselling as the primary intervention
options.rationale: Relationship support is a valuable addition when conflict is prominent but it does not treat a depressive episode with biological features, and offering it alone frames a clinical illness as a couple problem. Couple focused therapy is best considered once both partners' individual treatment is under way. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline

options.text: Notify child protection services because of the reported irritability
options.rationale: Irritability and snapping at family members in the context of a treatable depressive illness does not meet a threshold for statutory notification, and reporting at this point would damage the therapeutic relationship without protecting anyone. A notification obligation arises if there is a reasonable belief that a child is at risk of significant harm. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline

explanation.summary: Perinatal depression in fathers affects roughly 5 to 10 per cent of new fathers and peaks in the first six months after birth, yet it is screened for far less consistently than maternal depression and presents differently, with irritability, anger, withdrawal into work, risk taking and increased alcohol use often more prominent than expressed sadness. Australian guidance now recommends considering the mental health of both parents across the perinatal period, and the Edinburgh scale can be used with fathers although a lower cut off is applied because men score lower at equivalent severity. The strongest single risk factor is depression in the mother, which means a mother diagnosed with postnatal depression should prompt an enquiry about her partner rather than the reverse. Treating the father matters for outcomes beyond his own wellbeing, since paternal depression is independently associated with child emotional and behavioural difficulties and with a slower maternal recovery.
key_points: Paternal perinatal depression affects around 5 to 10 per cent of new fathers
Presentation skews towards irritability, withdrawal and increased alcohol use
The Edinburgh scale can be used in men with a lower cut off
Maternal depression is the strongest risk factor and should prompt enquiry
Paternal depression independently affects child outcomes and maternal recovery
explanation.pearls: A cut off of around 10 to 12 is generally used for fathers on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale rather than the 13 applied to mothers, so a father scoring 11 who would be dismissed as subthreshold on the maternal cut off warrants a full assessment.

sources.label: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
BMJ Best Practice: Paternal perinatal depression

subtopic_detail: A wife who has lost 6 kg and sleeps in a chair by the door because her husband with dementia wanders at night, presenting about her own back pain
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 74 year old woman who has come about persistent low back pain. Her husband, who has moderate Alzheimer disease, sits in the waiting room with their daughter.

While examining her you notice she has lost 6 kg since her last visit eight months ago. When you ask how things are at home she says she manages. On further gentle enquiry she describes sleeping in an armchair by the front door for the past four months because her husband gets up and tries to leave during the night. She has stopped her swimming class and her weekly card game and has not seen her sister since Easter. She says she feels constantly on edge and guilty, cries most days and has thought that her husband would be better off without her being so short tempered. She denies any thoughts of harming herself or him and is adamant she will not consider residential care.

data_table.Examination: Weight loss of 6 kg over eight months, appears fatigued with dark circles, tender lumbar paraspinal muscles with full range of movement and no neurological deficit, tearful when discussing her husband, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, denies suicidal ideation on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), HbA1c within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Treat her back pain and arrange a carer assessment with respite and supports
options.rationale: Her back pain is the presenting complaint but the sleep deprivation, weight loss, social withdrawal and persistent low mood identify carer strain with a probable depressive episode, so management pairs analgesia with a formal carer assessment, referral for in home and overnight respite, a dementia service review of the night time wandering, and her own mental health follow up. Naming her as a patient in her own right is what unlocks the carer support services she is eligible for. (Source: RACGP: Supporting carers of people with dementia)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting carers of people with dementia

options.text: Treat the back pain and review her again in three months as planned
options.rationale: Addressing only the presenting complaint misses the reason she has lost 6 kg and stopped everything she used to enjoy, and carers commonly present with somatic problems rather than naming their distress. Routine review alone would be appropriate if her mood, weight and social engagement were intact. (Source: RACGP: Supporting carers of people with dementia)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting carers of people with dementia

options.text: Prescribe a sedative for her husband so that she can sleep at night
options.rationale: Sedating a person with dementia to manage a carer's sleep carries a recognised risk of falls, further confusion and increased mortality, and non-pharmacological approaches to night time wandering such as environmental modification, door alarms and daytime activity should come first. Medication for behavioural symptoms is a last resort after a structured behavioural assessment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange urgent permanent residential placement for her husband this week
options.rationale: She has clearly declined residential care and forcing the issue at a first conversation risks her disengaging from services altogether, when respite and in home support may keep the arrangement viable. Permanent placement is a decision reached over time with the family once supports have been trialled, or urgently if the situation becomes unsafe. (Source: RACGP: Supporting carers of people with dementia)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting carers of people with dementia

options.text: Refer her for an urgent psychiatric admission because of her guilt and crying
options.rationale: She has no suicidal ideation, no psychotic features and retains function despite considerable strain, so inpatient admission is disproportionate and would remove the only carer her husband has. Admission would be indicated by active suicidal intent, psychosis or an inability to care for herself. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

explanation.summary: Around a million Australians provide unpaid care and carers of people with dementia carry among the highest burden, with rates of depression and anxiety substantially above those of the general population of the same age. Carers characteristically present with somatic complaints rather than psychological ones, and their distress surfaces only if the clinician asks directly about sleep, weight, social contact and how they are coping, which is why the opportunistic enquiry during an unrelated consultation is so productive. Night time behavioural symptoms are one of the strongest predictors of both carer breakdown and transition to residential care, so addressing wandering with environmental measures, daytime activity, review of medications and overnight respite is often the most effective single intervention. In Australia, practical supports are accessed through My Aged Care assessment, Carer Gateway and dementia specific services, and eligibility hinges on the carer being identified as such in the record. The statement that her husband would be better off without her requires careful exploration, since expressions of being a burden in a distressed carer can carry suicidal intent that is easily missed.
key_points: Carers present with somatic complaints; distress emerges only on direct enquiry
Sleep deprivation, weight loss and social withdrawal quantify the strain
Night time behavioural symptoms strongly predict carer breakdown and placement
Sedating the person with dementia to protect carer sleep carries real harms
Identifying her as a carer in the record unlocks assessment and respite
explanation.pearls: Statements such as he would be better off without me should always be explored explicitly for suicidal intent rather than accepted as self criticism, because older carers who express feeling a burden carry a suicide risk well above that of their age peers and the phrasing is easily heard as guilt alone.

sources.label: RACGP: Supporting carers of people with dementia
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

subtopic_detail: Episodes of watching himself from outside his body with the world looking flat and two dimensional, while knowing the experience is not real
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 24 year old man referred with episodes he finds terrifying. For the past eight months, several times a week, he feels as though he is watching himself from a short distance behind his own head, and the world around him looks flat, two dimensional and somehow artificial.

The episodes last from twenty minutes to several hours. Throughout them he knows the experience is not real and describes it as feeling like a documentary about his own life. There is no palpitation, chest tightness or shortness of breath and no fear of dying during them, and they are not confined to any particular place or situation. He has no memory gaps, no loss of time and no motor or sensory symptoms. He has never used cannabis or other drugs and drinks alcohol rarely. He has a history of significant emotional neglect in childhood. His magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and electroencephalogram were reported as normal.

data_table.Examination: Anxious but coherent, affect reactive, thought form normal with no formal thought disorder, no hallucinations, insight fully retained regarding the unreality of the experiences, cognition intact with a Mini-Mental State Examination of 30 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain reported as normal, electroencephalogram reported as normal including a sleep deprived recording, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, urine drug screen negative, full blood count and biochemistry within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start an antipsychotic, as the experiences indicate an emerging psychosis
options.rationale: Psychosis involves loss of insight into the unreality of the experience, and he consistently knows that what he describes is not real, which is the defining distinction. Antipsychotics are not an established treatment for this condition and expose him to metabolic and movement adverse effects. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for psychological therapy with psychoeducation about the symptoms
options.rationale: Persistent experiences of detachment from self and surroundings with intact insight, in the absence of substance use, seizures or a panic syndrome, identify depersonalisation-derealisation disorder, and the evidence supports psychoeducation with cognitive behavioural approaches that reduce symptom monitoring and catastrophic interpretation, alongside treatment of comorbid anxiety or depression. Explaining that the symptom is a recognised dissociative phenomenon rather than a sign of impending madness is itself therapeutic, because fear of the symptom perpetuates it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start an antiepileptic after repeating the electroencephalogram with video
options.rationale: Temporal lobe seizures can produce derealisation but characteristically last seconds to a couple of minutes, often with an olfactory or gustatory aura, automatisms or postictal confusion, none of which he describes during episodes lasting hours. His imaging and sleep deprived recording were both normal. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Depersonalisation-derealisation disorder)

options.text: Treat him for panic disorder with an antidepressant and interoceptive exposure
options.rationale: Depersonalisation commonly occurs during panic attacks, but panic requires a crescendo of autonomic symptoms with fear of catastrophe, and he has no palpitation, breathlessness or fear of dying and the episodes last hours rather than peaking within ten minutes. Where the two coexist, treating the panic does resolve the dissociation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange assessment for dissociative identity disorder with a specialist service
options.rationale: That diagnosis requires distinct identity states with associated amnesia, and he reports no memory gaps or lost time despite a history of childhood adversity. The near pair here is that both are dissociative disorders, but identity disruption with amnesia is absent. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Depersonalisation-derealisation disorder)

explanation.summary: Transient depersonalisation is extremely common, reported by up to half of the population at some point and particularly during sleep deprivation, acute stress or cannabis use, but as a persistent distressing disorder it affects roughly 1 to 2 per cent and is substantially under-recognised. The cardinal feature that separates it from psychosis is preserved reality testing: the person knows the experience is not real, which is why the as if quality of their description matters so much diagnostically. The differential requires exclusion of substance effects, particularly cannabis and ketamine, temporal lobe epilepsy where episodes are brief and stereotyped with other ictal features, panic disorder where dissociation rides on an autonomic surge, and post-traumatic and other dissociative disorders. Childhood emotional neglect and abuse are the strongest developmental risk factors. Treatment is psychological rather than pharmacological, and a substantial part of the benefit comes from explanation, because patients commonly fear they are going mad and that fear drives the symptom monitoring which perpetuates the condition.
key_points: Preserved insight into unreality separates this from psychosis
Exclude cannabis and ketamine use, temporal lobe seizures and panic disorder
Ictal derealisation lasts seconds to minutes, not hours
Childhood emotional neglect is the strongest developmental risk factor
Treatment is psychological; explanation alone reduces symptom perpetuation
explanation.pearls: Patients almost always describe the experience with an as if construction, such as as if I am watching myself, and that grammatical hedge is the clinical marker of retained reality testing; a patient who states without qualification that they genuinely are outside their body has crossed into psychosis and the diagnosis changes.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Trauma and dissociation resources
BMJ Best Practice: Depersonalisation-derealisation disorder

subtopic_detail: Prolonged thrashing episodes with eyes squeezed shut and preserved awareness afterwards in a woman already on two antiepileptic drugs
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar asked to see a 29 year old woman on the neurology ward, admitted after three prolonged episodes in a week. She carries a diagnosis of epilepsy made four years ago and takes levetiracetam and lamotrigine, both at therapeutic doses.

The nursing staff describe episodes lasting eight to fifteen minutes in which she thrashes her limbs asymmetrically, moves her pelvis forward and back, and rolls from side to side with her eyes squeezed tightly shut. She resists attempts to open her eyelids. Afterwards she is tearful and can recount what staff said during the episode. There is no tongue biting, no incontinence and no postictal confusion, and her serum lactate taken four minutes after the last episode was within normal limits. Video electroencephalography captured two typical episodes with no epileptiform change before, during or after either, and a normal posterior rhythm throughout.

data_table.Examination: Between episodes alert and oriented with normal neurological examination, no focal deficit, no tongue laceration, no injuries from the episodes
data_table.Investigations: Video electroencephalography capturing two typical episodes with no ictal or postictal epileptiform change and preserved posterior rhythm, serum lactate within normal limits four minutes after an episode, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain reported as normal, levetiracetam and lamotrigine levels both within the therapeutic range, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange a saline injection to provoke an event and confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Deceptive provocation damages the therapeutic relationship that the explanation of the diagnosis depends upon, and it is not required when typical events have already been captured on video. Provocation, if used at all, is performed openly with consent using suggestion rather than a sham injection. (Source: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement)
source_refs: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement

options.text: Tell her the tests are normal and discharge her to her general practitioner
options.rationale: Communicating only that tests are normal leaves her without a diagnosis to make sense of real and disabling symptoms, and this pattern of communication predicts repeat presentations and poorer outcomes. A positive diagnostic label delivered with an explanation of mechanism is what changes the trajectory. (Source: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement)
source_refs: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement

options.text: Treat her for factitious disorder and notify her driving licence authority
options.rationale: Functional seizures are not consciously produced and labelling them as feigned is both inaccurate and harmful to engagement. Driving restrictions do still apply to unexplained loss of control of a vehicle and are discussed openly with her, but that is a separate matter from a diagnosis of deliberate deception. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)

options.text: Add a third antiepileptic drug and refer for epilepsy surgery assessment
options.rationale: Escalating antiepileptic treatment for events that are not epileptic adds side effects without benefit and reinforces an incorrect diagnosis. Surgical assessment is for drug resistant focal epilepsy with a demonstrated epileptogenic zone, which the video recording specifically excludes here. (Source: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement)
source_refs: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement

options.text: Explain the diagnosis positively and plan supervised antiepileptic withdrawal
options.rationale: Typical events captured on video electroencephalography without any electrographic correlate establish functional seizures, and the single most important therapeutic step is a clear positive explanation of the diagnosis, framed as a recognised condition that is real and treatable rather than as an absence of disease, followed by planned withdrawal of unnecessary antiepileptic drugs and referral for psychological therapy. A significant minority stop having events after the explanation alone. (Source: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement)
source_refs: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement

explanation.summary: Functional seizures, also called dissociative or psychogenic non-epileptic seizures, account for roughly 20 to 30 per cent of patients referred to specialist epilepsy services and are frequently misdiagnosed as drug resistant epilepsy, with the average delay to correct diagnosis measured in years and considerable iatrogenic harm from antiepileptic drugs and intensive care admissions for apparent status. Semiological features that favour a functional mechanism include prolonged duration beyond two minutes, asynchronous or thrashing limb movements, pelvic thrusting, side to side head rolling, eye closure with resistance to opening, preserved awareness or recall of the event, absence of postictal confusion, and a lactate that fails to rise after an apparently generalised convulsion. None of these is individually diagnostic, which is why video electroencephalography capturing a typical event remains the reference standard. Management begins with how the diagnosis is delivered, since a positive explanation that validates the reality of the symptoms while naming the mechanism is associated with better outcomes than a statement that investigations are normal, and it is followed by withdrawal of unnecessary antiepileptic drugs and psychological therapy, with cognitive behavioural approaches having the best evidence.
key_points: Functional seizures account for a fifth to a third of specialist epilepsy referrals
Prolonged asynchronous events with forced eye closure and preserved recall are suggestive
A lactate that does not rise after an apparent convulsion argues against epilepsy
Video electroencephalography capturing a typical event is the reference standard
How the diagnosis is delivered is itself a determinant of outcome
explanation.pearls: Serum lactate rises within minutes after a genuine generalised tonic-clonic seizure and typically normalises by about an hour, so a sample taken within 10 to 15 minutes of an apparent convulsion that shows a normal lactate is strong evidence against a generalised epileptic event; a sample taken two hours later proves nothing.

sources.label: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement
Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive
BMJ Best Practice: Dissociative seizures

subtopic_detail: A man convinced he has motor neurone disease after eleven months of normal investigations who examines his own tongue daily and requests another neurology opinion
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 41 year old man who is convinced he has motor neurone disease. He has been preoccupied with this for eleven months, since a colleague of similar age was diagnosed.

He examines his tongue in the mirror several times a day looking for twitching, photographs his calf muscles weekly to compare them, and spends two to three hours most evenings reading patient forums. He has seen two neurologists privately; both documented a normal examination and normal nerve conduction and electromyography studies, the most recent six weeks ago. He accepts that the tests were normal but says they may have been done too early to show anything. He has taken three weeks of leave and has stopped going to the gym for fear of accelerating muscle loss. He is now asking for a third neurology referral and for a repeat of the electromyography.

data_table.Examination: Normal bulk and tone throughout with power 5 out of 5 in all muscle groups, no fasciculation observed including in the tongue, reflexes normal and symmetrical with downgoing plantar responses, no bulbar signs, gait normal, weight stable
data_table.Investigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography reported as normal on two occasions, the most recent six weeks ago; creatine kinase 118 U/L (less than 200); thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits; full blood count and biochemistry within normal limits; magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and cervical spine reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Arrange the third neurology opinion he requests to provide reassurance
options.rationale: Repeated specialist opinions provide only transient relief and then strengthen the belief that something remains undetected, so each one entrenches the illness behaviour. A further opinion is warranted only if new objective signs emerge on examination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Repeat the electromyography now to settle the question definitively
options.rationale: Repeating a normal test in the absence of new clinical findings cannot settle the question, because the concern is not about the result but about the possibility that disease is not yet detectable. Reinvestigation also validates the checking behaviour that maintains the disorder. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Consolidate his care with one clinician and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: Persistent disease preoccupation with checking and reassurance seeking despite appropriate normal investigation is illness anxiety disorder, and management consolidates care with a single clinician offering regular scheduled appointments not contingent on symptoms, sets an explicit agreement to stop further investigation without new signs, and refers for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting the checking and catastrophic interpretation. The reality of his distress is acknowledged explicitly while the focus shifts from finding disease to reducing preoccupation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Tell him firmly that there is nothing wrong and decline further appointments
options.rationale: Blunt dismissal with withdrawal of care typically drives the person to other providers and further investigation elsewhere, fragmenting their care and increasing iatrogenic risk. The therapeutic move is regular scheduled contact with one clinician rather than reduced access. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start an antipsychotic, as his fixed belief about the diagnosis is delusional
options.rationale: A delusion is held with unshakeable conviction despite contrary evidence, whereas he accepts the tests were normal and worries that disease may not yet be detectable, which is anxious doubt rather than fixed false belief. That distinction is what separates illness anxiety disorder from a somatic delusional disorder, where antipsychotic treatment would be appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Illness anxiety disorder is characterised by preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness, with either minimal somatic symptoms or symptoms grossly disproportionate to the concern, persisting for at least six months and accompanied by either excessive health related behaviours or maladaptive avoidance. It is distinguished from somatic symptom disorder, in which distressing physical symptoms are prominent, and from a somatic delusional disorder, in which the belief is held with delusional conviction rather than anxious uncertainty. The therapeutic paradox at the centre of management is that reassurance and reinvestigation reduce anxiety for hours to days and then increase it, so each cycle of testing makes the disorder worse while appearing kind in the moment. Effective management consolidates care with one clinician using regular appointments scheduled by time rather than triggered by symptoms, agrees explicit criteria for further investigation, and refers for cognitive behavioural therapy, which has the strongest evidence; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors help where there is comorbid depression or where therapy alone is insufficient. Clinicians must also remain alert to genuine disease developing, which is why the agreement is framed around new objective findings rather than a blanket refusal ever to investigate again.
key_points: Preoccupation with illness for six months or more with checking or avoidance defines it
Reassurance and repeat testing worsen the disorder over time
One coordinating clinician with time based appointments is the structural intervention
Cognitive behavioural therapy has the strongest evidence; antidepressants help if comorbid
Anxious doubt distinguishes this from a somatic delusional disorder
explanation.pearls: Scheduling appointments by the calendar rather than by symptoms is the specific manoeuvre that breaks the cycle, because a fortnightly appointment that happens regardless of how he feels removes the incentive for symptom escalation as the route to being seen.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
RACGP: Managing medically unexplained symptoms in general practice
BMJ Best Practice: Illness anxiety disorder

subtopic_detail: Elation, pressured speech and reduced need for sleep starting five days after prednisolone was increased for a vasculitis flare
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar asked to see a 52 year old woman on the renal ward. She was admitted five days ago with a flare of microscopic polyangiitis and her prednisolone was increased from 10 mg to 75 mg daily, with pulsed methylprednisolone on the first two days.

The nursing staff report she has slept about two hours a night for three nights without appearing tired, has been telephoning relatives at 3 am with plans to sell her house, and has been talking so rapidly that they struggle to interrupt her. She is elated and irritable by turns. She has no personal or family history of mood disorder. On examination she is overfamiliar with flight of ideas and grandiose plans but is fully oriented, attentive on digit span, and her Mini-Mental State Examination is 29 out of 30. There is no fluctuation in her conscious level, no visual hallucination and no asterixis.

data_table.Examination: Elated and irritable by turns, overfamiliar, pressured speech that is difficult to interrupt, flight of ideas, grandiose plans, fully oriented with intact attention on digit span, Mini-Mental State Examination 29 out of 30, no fluctuating conscious level, no visual hallucinations, no asterixis or myoclonus
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45 to 90), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.20 to 2.60), glucose 11.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 7.8), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, C reactive protein 18 mg/L (less than 5) down from 96 mg/L, urine culture no growth, computed tomography of the brain reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Treat this as hyperactive delirium and search for an occult infection
options.rationale: Delirium requires disturbance of attention and awareness with a fluctuating course, and she is fully oriented with intact attention on digit span and no fluctuation in conscious level. Her inflammatory markers are falling and her urine culture is negative, so an occult infection is unlikely to be driving this. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start an antidepressant, as grandiosity in this setting reflects agitated depression
options.rationale: Elation with reduced need for sleep, pressured speech and grandiosity is an elevated mood state, and an antidepressant would be expected to worsen it. Corticosteroids can also precipitate depression, but that presents with low mood and psychomotor slowing rather than this picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Give regular diazepam alone and review her again in seventy two hours
options.rationale: A benzodiazepine may be a useful adjunct for sedation and sleep but does not treat the manic syndrome itself, and using it alone for three days leaves her making high risk financial decisions. Benzodiazepine monotherapy is reasonable for short term management of anxiety or agitation without an affective syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Discuss steroid dose reduction with the renal team and start an antipsychotic
options.rationale: A first manic episode beginning days after high dose corticosteroid with no personal or family history of mood disorder indicates a corticosteroid induced mood disorder, and management combines review of the steroid dose with the treating team, reducing to the lowest dose that controls the vasculitis, with a short course of an antipsychotic such as olanzapine or quetiapine for symptom control. The steroid cannot simply be stopped because the underlying vasculitis is being actively treated, which is why this is a negotiation with the renal team rather than a unilateral decision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start lithium as maintenance treatment for a first episode of bipolar disorder
options.rationale: Lithium is a treatment for primary bipolar disorder and long term maintenance is not indicated for an episode precipitated by an identified and removable cause. Her impaired renal function also makes lithium a poor choice on safety grounds. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Corticosteroid induced psychiatric disturbance is common, affecting a substantial minority of patients on high dose treatment, and the risk rises steeply above the equivalent of about 40 mg of prednisolone daily. Elevated mood, insomnia and irritability dominate in the first weeks while depression is more characteristic of prolonged treatment or of dose reduction, and frank psychosis and delirium also occur. The syndrome is usually dose related and reversible, and the most important step is to review the steroid dose with the team treating the underlying disease, since abrupt cessation is often unsafe and the right answer is the lowest dose that controls the primary condition. Symptomatic treatment with a second generation antipsychotic is preferred to lithium or valproate for a drug induced episode, particularly where renal or hepatic function is impaired, and prophylaxis should be considered in someone who has previously reacted to corticosteroids and needs a further course. Practical protection also matters, because patients in this state can make irreversible financial and interpersonal decisions during an episode that lasts only days.
key_points: Risk rises above the equivalent of about 40 mg prednisolone daily
Elevated mood and insomnia dominate early; depression is later or on withdrawal
Intact attention and no fluctuation separate this from hyperactive delirium
Review the dose with the treating team rather than stopping the steroid
A second generation antipsychotic is preferred to lithium, especially in renal impairment
explanation.pearls: A patient who has had a corticosteroid induced mood episode has roughly a 50 per cent chance of recurrence with a subsequent high dose course, so the episode is documented prominently and prophylactic olanzapine or quetiapine is considered from day one of any future pulse rather than waiting for symptoms.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
Australian Medicines Handbook: Corticosteroids
BMJ Best Practice: Corticosteroid induced psychiatric disorders

subtopic_detail: Small figures seen at the end of the bed in a man with a four year tremor and shuffling gait whose levodopa was increased last month
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 76 year old man in a community clinic with his wife. He has had a resting tremor and shuffling gait for four years and his levodopa with carbidopa was increased four weeks ago because of worsening mobility.

Since then he has seen small figures of children standing at the end of his bed in the evening, and last week he saw a cat walk across the lounge room. He initially knew they were not real but is now becoming frightened and has begun accusing his wife of letting people into the house. His wife says his memory is mildly affected but that his alertness varies through the day. On examination he has a pill rolling tremor, cogwheel rigidity and a shuffling gait with reduced arm swing. His Mini-Mental State Examination is 24 out of 30. Urinalysis shows no nitrites or leucocytes and his blood tests are unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Resting pill rolling tremor worse on the right, cogwheel rigidity at both wrists, hypomimia, shuffling gait with reduced right arm swing, Mini-Mental State Examination 24 out of 30, no focal neurological deficit, no nystagmus
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis with no nitrites or leucocytes and urine culture pending with no growth at 24 hours, full blood count within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, corrected calcium within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor and make no change to his current treatment
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors do have a genuine role in the cognitive and psychotic symptoms of Lewy body and Parkinson disease dementia and are worth considering, but leaving a recently increased dopaminergic dose unchanged ignores the most likely precipitant. Reviewing the temporally related drug change comes first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Treat empirically for a urinary tract infection and reassess in three days
options.rationale: Infection is always worth excluding as a precipitant of psychosis in an older person, but his urinalysis is bland, his inflammatory markers are normal and his culture has shown no growth. Empirical antibiotics would treat nothing while the dopaminergic precipitant continued. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start risperidone at a low dose and review him again in one week
options.rationale: Risperidone has substantial dopamine D2 blocking activity and reliably worsens parkinsonian motor features, and in this population it also carries the risk of severe antipsychotic sensitivity reactions. It is a reasonable choice for psychosis in someone without a parkinsonian syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Give haloperidol as required for the frightening visual hallucinations
options.rationale: A high potency first generation antipsychotic is the most hazardous option here, capable of precipitating marked rigidity, immobility and neuroleptic malignant syndrome in a patient with a parkinsonian disorder. Haloperidol retains a limited role in hyperactive delirium in patients without parkinsonism or Lewy body pathology. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Review his antiparkinsonian medications and reduce the dopaminergic load
options.rationale: Visual hallucinations beginning four weeks after a dopaminergic dose increase point first to the medication, so the initial step is a systematic review that withdraws adjuncts with a poor ratio of benefit to psychiatric risk such as anticholinergics, amantadine and dopamine agonists, then reduces levodopa to the lowest dose giving acceptable mobility. Where psychosis persists after that, quetiapine or clozapine are the antipsychotics used because they have the least effect on motor function. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Psychosis affects a large proportion of people with Parkinson disease over the course of their illness and is one of the strongest predictors of nursing home placement and carer breakdown. Visual hallucinations are the characteristic symptom, often beginning as well formed images of people or animals with insight preserved, and progressing to loss of insight with delusions, most commonly of infidelity or of intruders. Contributors are both the disease itself, with Lewy body pathology and cholinergic deficit, and dopaminergic treatment, so the assessment always begins by excluding an intercurrent illness and then reviewing the drug chart, withdrawing agents in order of psychiatric risk relative to motor benefit before reducing levodopa. Where an antipsychotic is needed, the choice is constrained to quetiapine or clozapine, since all agents with meaningful D2 blockade worsen motor function and people with Lewy body pathology can suffer severe sensitivity reactions with marked rigidity and a mortality risk. The overlap with dementia with Lewy bodies is considerable, and fluctuating alertness with early visual hallucinations and parkinsonism should prompt consideration of that diagnosis, for which cholinesterase inhibitors are particularly useful.
key_points: Visual hallucinations of people or animals are the characteristic symptom
Exclude intercurrent illness, then review the drug chart before adding anything
Withdraw anticholinergics, amantadine and agonists before reducing levodopa
Only quetiapine and clozapine are acceptable antipsychotics in this population
Fluctuating alertness with early hallucinations suggests dementia with Lewy bodies
explanation.pearls: Severe antipsychotic sensitivity occurs in roughly half of people with Lewy body pathology given a D2 blocking agent and carries a two to threefold increase in mortality, so a single dose of haloperidol given overnight for agitation can leave a previously mobile patient rigid and bedbound.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
BMJ Best Practice: Parkinson disease psychosis

subtopic_detail: Crying that starts and stops abruptly without sadness between episodes in a man eight weeks after a left hemisphere stroke
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 68 year old man in a rehabilitation unit eight weeks after a left middle cerebral artery infarct that left him with a mild right hemiparesis and mild expressive dysphasia. The team has asked whether he is depressed.

His wife reports that he bursts into tears several times a day, often when greeted by a visitor or during a television advertisement, and that the crying stops as abruptly as it starts. He tells you through his dysphasia that he is not sad and finds the crying embarrassing and out of proportion to how he feels. Between episodes he is engaged in therapy, has a good appetite, sleeps well and looks forward to his grandchildren's visits. He has made steady gains in physiotherapy and has not lost interest in anything. He takes aspirin, atorvastatin and perindopril.

data_table.Examination: Mild right hemiparesis with power 4 out of 5 in the right arm and leg, mild expressive dysphasia with preserved comprehension, abrupt onset and offset crying episodes during the interview with rapid return to baseline affect, no psychomotor retardation, no anhedonia elicited on questioning through his wife and by nodding responses
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, HbA1c 6.2 per cent (less than 6.0), computed tomography of the brain showing an established left middle cerebral artery territory infarct

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Explain the symptom and start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
options.rationale: Abrupt stereotyped crying triggered by minor stimuli with no sustained low mood or anhedonia between episodes is emotionalism after stroke rather than a depressive episode, and it responds to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors at lower doses and within days rather than the weeks needed for depression. Explanation to the patient and family is a substantial part of treatment because the symptom is distressing largely through being misread as uncontrollable grief. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Start an antidepressant at full dose for a moderate post-stroke depression
options.rationale: Post-stroke depression is common and would require persistent low mood or anhedonia, and he specifically denies sadness and remains engaged, eating, sleeping and looking forward to visits. The distinction matters because emotionalism responds to lower doses and much more quickly. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Refer for grief focused psychological therapy to process his disability
options.rationale: Adjustment to disability after stroke is real and therapy can help with it, but this symptom has a neurological mechanism and does not resolve with psychological processing of loss. His expressive dysphasia would also limit a purely verbal therapy as the primary approach. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Reassure the team that the crying needs no treatment and will settle over time
options.rationale: Although emotionalism does improve over months in many patients, it causes significant embarrassment and social withdrawal and interferes with rehabilitation participation, and effective treatment is available. Watchful waiting is reasonable only for mild infrequent episodes that the patient and family find tolerable once explained. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Start a low dose antipsychotic to control the emotional lability directly
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have no role in this symptom and add sedation, falls risk and extrapyramidal effects in an older patient in active rehabilitation. They would be considered for psychotic symptoms or severe agitation, neither of which is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Three distinct emotional syndromes follow stroke and are routinely conflated: post-stroke depression, which affects roughly a third of survivors and requires sustained low mood or anhedonia with the usual biological features; emotionalism, a disorder of the expression rather than the experience of emotion, with abrupt episodes triggered by trivial stimuli, little corresponding subjective feeling and rapid return to baseline; and apathy, with reduced initiation and motivation in the absence of sadness, which families frequently report as depression. The distinction is practical rather than academic, because emotionalism responds to serotonergic antidepressants at doses lower than those used for depression and within a few days to a fortnight, whereas depression needs full therapeutic dosing over weeks and apathy responds poorly to antidepressants. Screening for mood after stroke is recommended in Australian guidelines, and dysphasia complicates it, requiring observer rated tools and collateral history rather than self report questionnaires alone. Left untreated, emotionalism restricts social contact and rehabilitation participation because patients avoid situations in which they expect to cry.
key_points: Emotionalism affects expression rather than experience of emotion
Abrupt onset and offset with no sustained sadness is the discriminating pattern
It responds to serotonergic antidepressants at lower doses and within days
Apathy after stroke is a third syndrome commonly mislabelled as depression
Dysphasia mandates observer rated tools and collateral history for mood screening
explanation.pearls: The response of emotionalism to a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is typically apparent within 3 to 7 days, so a lack of any change in crying frequency after two weeks should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis rather than the dose escalation that would be appropriate in depression.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
Cochrane Review: Interventions for emotionalism after stroke

subtopic_detail: Choosing analgesia for a fractured ankle in a man taking an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor whose last dose was this morning
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 44 year old man who fell from a ladder two hours ago and has a closed displaced ankle fracture requiring operative fixation later today. He is in severe pain rated 8 out of 10.

He has treatment resistant depression and has taken tranylcypromine 30 mg daily for the past eight months, having failed four previous antidepressant trials, with the best response of his life on this drug. His last dose was this morning. He takes no other regular medication and follows a low tyramine diet. His observations are pulse 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in air and temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. He is fully alert with no head injury and no neurovascular deficit distal to the fracture. The orthopaedic registrar has asked you to provide analgesia now and the anaesthetist is asking whether the antidepressant should be stopped before theatre.

data_table.Examination: Closed displaced right ankle fracture with intact skin, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses present with normal capillary refill and preserved sensation, fully alert with Glasgow Coma Scale 15, no head or spinal injury, no clonus, no hyperreflexia, pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, ankle radiographs showing a displaced bimalleolar fracture, electrocardiogram showing sinus rhythm with a QTc of 410 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to his analgesia and perioperative antidepressant management?

options.text: Give fentanyl now and postpone surgery for two weeks after stopping the drug
options.rationale: Fentanyl is a reasonable non-serotonergic choice, but delaying fixation of a displaced ankle fracture for two weeks to wash out the antidepressant would cause malunion, prolonged pain and immobility for a theoretical anaesthetic convenience. The interaction is managed by drug selection rather than by deferring necessary surgery. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management scientific evidence)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management scientific evidence

options.text: Give pethidine now and stop the antidepressant until after his operation
